description: M:N threading + modern runtime threading decomposed. Go's goroutines + GMP model. Java's virtual threads (Project Loom). Erlang's BEAM. The shared insight: many lightweight tasks multiplexed onto few kernel threads via a runtime scheduler that handles blocking. The mechanisms: park/unpark, work stealing, netpoller for I/O, preemption tricks, stack management.

sub_mechanisms.name: goroutine
sub_mechanisms.definition: Go's user-space lightweight thread. Tiny initial stack (2 KB); grows on demand. Scheduled by Go runtime, not OS.
sub_mechanisms.why: Cheap: millions of goroutines on a single process. The Go runtime's scheduler maps them to OS threads. The unit of concurrency in Go programs.

sub_mechanisms.name: Go_GMP_model
sub_mechanisms.definition: G = goroutine, M = OS thread, P = processor (logical scheduling slot). P holds a run queue of G; M executes G via P. ~GOMAXPROCS Ps total.
sub_mechanisms.why: Scales threading to many goroutines on few cores. P is the unit of parallelism (one runnable G per P at a time). M may detach from P during blocking syscalls; another M picks up the P.

sub_mechanisms.name: goroutine_park_unpark
sub_mechanisms.definition: park: G stops running, M can pick up another G. unpark: G becomes runnable again, queued on a P.
sub_mechanisms.why: Cooperative scheduling primitive. Blocking on channel = park; channel send to waiter = unpark. Cost: ~50-100ns per pair. Foundation of all Go synchronisation.

sub_mechanisms.name: netpoller
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-runtime poll mechanism (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD) that wakes goroutines blocked on I/O.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets blocking-style I/O (n, err := conn.Read(buf)) run on millions of goroutines without each consuming an OS thread. The poller handles all sockets in one goroutine; ready sockets' goroutines wake up. Foundation of Go's network performance.

sub_mechanisms.name: preemptive_goroutine_scheduling
sub_mechanisms.definition: Go 1.14+: compiler inserts preemption checks at function calls; long-running CPU-bound goroutines can be preempted by SIGURG signal.
sub_mechanisms.why: Pre-1.14: tight loops with no function calls could starve other goroutines. Post-1.14: asynchronous preemption handles this. Critical for fair scheduling.

sub_mechanisms.name: goroutine_stack_growth
sub_mechanisms.definition: Initial stack: 2 KB. On stack overflow check, runtime allocates larger stack + copies current frames.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets million-goroutine workloads fit in memory. Trade-off: copy cost on growth (mitigated by exponential expansion + segmented stacks in some versions). Stack scanning during GC: roots include all goroutine stacks.

sub_mechanisms.name: virtual_thread_loom
sub_mechanisms.definition: JVM's Project Loom (Java 21+): lightweight threads scheduled on a small pool of carrier threads.
sub_mechanisms.why: Java's response to Go's goroutines + Kotlin's coroutines. Same code style (blocking I/O) works without blocking OS threads. Continuations (also added) are the underlying primitive.

sub_mechanisms.name: continuation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Captured execution state (program counter + stack frames) that can be resumed. Loom's foundation.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets a virtual thread suspend + resume on any code line. Implementation: stack frames moved to heap on yield; restored on resume. Generalises threading to first-class continuations (Scheme's call/cc was first; Loom brings it to JVM).

sub_mechanisms.name: Erlang_BEAM_scheduler
sub_mechanisms.definition: Erlang's runtime uses N schedulers (typically one per core). Each schedules N actors (processes in BEAM terminology). Pre-emptive within actor (counts reductions).
sub_mechanisms.why: Designed for telecom: 100K+ actors per node. Strong isolation between actors (no shared state — only message passing). Reduction-based preemption ensures fairness even within long computations.

sub_mechanisms.name: actor_model
sub_mechanisms.definition: Concurrency model: actors are isolated units communicating only via messages. No shared mutable state.
sub_mechanisms.why: Eliminates many concurrency bugs (no shared state = no data races). Erlang, Akka (Scala/Java), Pony all use this. Cost: message-passing overhead vs shared memory. Different trade than goroutines (which share memory).

sub_mechanisms.name: async_runtime_tokio
sub_mechanisms.definition: Rust's tokio: async runtime with multi-threaded scheduler. Tasks are stateful async fns; runtime polls them when ready.
sub_mechanisms.why: Different model from Go: cooperative multitasking via async/await. No preemption — task yields at .await points. Tasks are typically smaller than goroutines (no per-task stack); scheduling is more explicit.

sub_mechanisms.name: task_polling
sub_mechanisms.definition: Async runtimes poll a task's future. Future returns Pending (not ready) or Ready (with value). Runtime suspends Pending tasks until wake notification.
sub_mechanisms.why: The async model's core mechanism. Different from threading: no thread is 'blocked' — the task is paused as a state machine. Wakers connect external events (I/O completion) back to runtime.

derivation_rules.name: M_N_threading_amortises_thread_creation
if: a runtime multiplexes many user-tasks onto few OS threads
then: per-task creation + switching cost is amortised
derivation_rules.why: OS thread create: ~50µs. Goroutine create: ~1µs. Switching: OS thread context switch ~1-2µs; goroutine switch ~100ns. Million-task workloads tractable only with M:N.

derivation_rules.name: netpoller_unblocks_blocking_style_IO
if: I/O syscalls would block the OS thread
then: the runtime intercepts + parks the goroutine until I/O ready
derivation_rules.why: Go's net.Conn.Read looks blocking but doesn't block the OS thread. Runtime registers interest via epoll; OS thread picks up another goroutine. When ready, the original goroutine is woken. Enables blocking-style code at non-blocking cost.

derivation_rules.name: preemption_prevents_cpu_bound_starvation
if: a long CPU-bound task runs in a cooperative runtime
derivation_rules.why: Cooperative scheduling assumes tasks yield. CPU-bound tasks don't. Go 1.14 added asynchronous preemption via signals; Loom uses similar tricks. Without it, single misbehaving task hangs the runtime.

derivation_rules.name: actor_isolation_eliminates_data_races
if: actors only communicate via message passing
then: data races are impossible by construction
derivation_rules.why: No shared state = no concurrent writes = no races. Erlang's reliability story rests on this. Cost: copying data on message send. Tradeoff: eliminates whole bug class at the cost of some overhead.

derivation_rules.name: async_task_lighter_than_goroutine
if: a task is purely state-machine-driven (no stack needed)
then: it has lower memory footprint than a stackful thread/goroutine
derivation_rules.why: Async task: small state (current state machine variant). Goroutine: ≥2 KB initial stack + bookkeeping. Async runtime supports more concurrent tasks at the cost of more explicit code (await markers).
